title: Marijuana for Sleep: What the Research Says
h1: Cannabis and Sleep: THC, CBD, CBN and What Studies Show
metaDescription: Marijuana for sleep, explained: how THC, CBD and CBN affect sleep, what studies show about tolerance and withdrawal, and how adults approach evening use.
excerpt: THC, CBD and CBN each touch sleep differently, and the research hasn't caught up with the marketing. Here's what studies show, where they fall short and when to talk to a doctor.
keyTakeaways: In lab studies, THC helped people fall asleep sooner and cut REM sleep, but regular use builds tolerance.
CBD findings vary with the dose and the study, and the studies behind them are small.
CBN's sleepy reputation outruns its evidence: one larger trial found fewer awakenings but no faster sleep.
Sleep trouble is among the most common problems when regular users stop.
Talk with a doctor first, especially if you take other medications or may have sleep apnea.
body:
Does marijuana for sleep live up to its reputation? The research is mixed. THC can help people fall asleep faster at first, but it reshapes sleep stages, and regular use builds tolerance. Studies of CBD and CBN are limited and point in different directions. Here's what the science shows, where it falls short and how adults approach evening use with care.

## Why marijuana for sleep is such a common question

Cannabis has a long reputation for causing drowsiness, and a 2020 review by National Institutes of Health researchers notes its growing use as a sleep aid. The evidence hasn't kept pace. A 2020 systematic review of 26 animal, lab and clinical studies found too little research to support routine clinical use of cannabinoids for any sleep disorder. It rated most of those studies at moderate to high risk of bias.

## THC and sleep: falling asleep vs. sleep stages

THC, the compound behind the high, has been studied for its effects on sleep since the early 1970s. Those early studies found that a dose of cannabis or THC helped people fall asleep sooner and cut time awake during the night. It also increased deep (slow-wave) sleep and reduced REM sleep, the stage most linked to vivid dreams.

There are two catches. Repeated use produces tolerance, including to those sleep effects. And people who use cannabis regularly show more disrupted sleep in studies, especially when they stop. Falling asleep faster tonight isn't the same as sleeping better for months.

## CBD and sleep: findings that vary by dose and study

CBD doesn't cause THC's high, and its sleep studies are small, with different doses and different people:

- In a small study published in 1981, people with insomnia who took 160 mg of CBD reported sleeping more than those given a placebo.
- In a 2020 lab study, 100 mg of CBD on its own didn't make infrequent cannabis users feel sleepier.
- In another study, CBD taken with THC pushed against THC's drowsiness, toward wakefulness.

So CBD's effects may depend on the dose and on what it's paired with, but no CBD dose has been shown to reliably improve sleep.

## CBN: hype vs. evidence

CBN (cannabinol) appears as THC ages and degrades, and it's often sold as the sleepy cannabinoid. A 2021 review found the evidence thin. Human studies were mostly small ones from the 1970s and 1980s, and it found no trials that measured sleep with validated questionnaires or overnight recordings. Sleep products, it noted, typically held 5 mg of CBN or less.

A later trial of 293 adults with poor sleep compared five nightly regimens over a week: a placebo, 20 mg of CBN alone, or CBN plus one of three CBD doses. Compared with the placebo, CBN alone reduced nighttime awakenings and overall sleep disturbance. No group fell asleep faster or felt less tired the next day, adding CBD didn't improve on CBN, and the main measure, sleep quality, fell short of statistical significance. The study was short and run by researchers who worked for cannabis companies. Our [CBN explainer](/blog/what-is-cbn-benefits-effects/) has more.

## Tolerance, rebound and withdrawal sleep problems

Researchers report altered sleep in most regular users who try to quit, and they call it one of the most consistent parts of cannabis withdrawal. In studies of heavy users during abstinence, people slept less, slept less efficiently and got less non-REM and REM sleep.

If you notice you need more to get the same effect, that's tolerance. A planned break is one way people reset, and our [guide to tolerance breaks](/blog/t-breaks-marijuana-tolerance/) shows how to plan one. If sleep stays rough after you stop, tell your doctor.

## How adults choose strains and products for evening use

No strain or product is proven to deliver better sleep, so read a nighttime label as the maker's intent, not a promise. Adults who use cannabis in the evening tend to weigh a few practical points:

- **Timing.** Inhaled cannabis is felt within minutes, while edibles start much later and last longer.
- **Amount.** Start small and give it time before deciding on more.
- **Labels.** Indica isn't a reliable guide to a plant's genetics, so many people check THC and CBD numbers instead. Our guide to [indica strains people choose at night](/blog/indica-strains-for-sleep/) explains why.
- **Mixing.** Many people keep cannabis apart from alcohol and other things that cause drowsiness.
- **Notes.** A short log of the product, the amount and how you slept shows patterns, including creeping tolerance.

For formats and routines, see our [guide to products people pick for bedtime](/blog/cannabis-products-for-sleep/) and our tips on [nighttime cannabis use](/blog/nighttime-cannabis-use/).

## Talking with a doctor, especially about other medications

Before using cannabis for sleep, talk with a doctor or pharmacist and bring a list of everything you take, including over-the-counter sleep aids. Ask about interactions with anything that also makes you drowsy.

Lasting sleep trouble can have causes worth finding, such as sleep apnea. In a 2018 position statement, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine said medical cannabis and its synthetic extracts shouldn't be used for obstructive sleep apnea, citing too little evidence of effectiveness, tolerability and safety. It urged people with sleep apnea to discuss their options with a licensed provider at an accredited sleep facility.

If you're pregnant or breastfeeding, skip cannabis and ask your clinician about other options. Our [patient guide](/patient-guide/) explains cannabinoids in more depth. In Michigan, cannabis is for adults 21 and older, or 18 and older with a medical marijuana card.

faq.q: Does weed help you sleep better?
faq.a: Not reliably, based on current research. THC can help some people fall asleep faster at first, but it reduces REM sleep and tolerance builds with regular use. A 2020 systematic review found too little good evidence to support routine use of cannabinoids for any sleep disorder. If poor sleep is a pattern, a doctor can help find the cause.

It can. THC tends to reduce REM sleep, the stage most tied to vivid dreaming, which may be one reason people remember fewer dreams after using it. In a small study published in 1981, CBD doses from 40 to 160 mg were also linked to less dream recall than a placebo.

faq.q: Is CBD or THC better for sleep?
faq.a: Neither has strong evidence behind it. THC can shorten the time it takes to fall asleep at first, but it cuts REM sleep and tolerance builds. CBD's findings vary with the dose and with whether it's taken alongside THC. Talk with a doctor before choosing either for sleep, especially if you take other medications.

faq.q: Can I become dependent on cannabis to sleep?
faq.a: It's possible. Regular use builds tolerance, so the same amount can do less over time, and researchers report sleep problems in most regular users who try to quit. That doesn't happen to everyone, but it's a good reason to keep use occasional, take planned breaks and talk with a doctor if you find you can't sleep without it.

review.notes: Writer: Medical article: no shop, menu, deals or rewards links, no shopping section, no product-helps-condition claims. The evening-use section lists practical choices only. The indica point is the settled Watts (2021) finding, carried by the linked indica article (6-source cap). The CBN trial's company affiliations are described without naming brands. Fact-check 2026-10-24: 32 claims, 5 fixed (CBN trial design was wrong: five arms, not CBN vs placebo; excerpt's 'research is younger than the marketing' was wrong; 'longest research record' unsupported; 'small' and 'shift with the dose' overstated). All 6 sources opened (E-utilities / Europe PMC) and support the text; extra checks against Harvey 1990, Spindle 2020, Nicholson 2004, CDC MMWR 2015, NICHD and FDA (cited here, not added: the 6-source cap is reached).
